t: “The actual significance of the word sáhitya [loosely, "literature"] is inherent in the word itself. Sáhitya is defined as 'that whose characteristic is to move with (sahita = ‘with’) the trends of lifeʼ… The word sáhitya can be interpreted in another way as well: sa + hita = hitena saha, 'that which co-exists with hita [welfare]ʼ. Where there is no inner spirit of welfare, we cannot use the term sáhitya. The creations or compositions of those who proclaim, ‘Art for artʼs sake,ʼ cannot be treated as sáhitya… Thus literature is that which moves together with society and leads society towards true fulfilment and welfare by providing the inspiration to serve. The statement ‘Art for artʼs sakeʼ is not acceptable; rather we should say, 'Art for service and blessedness.ʼ… Those who are inferior and neglected, helpless and destitute – whom society considers to be infernal maggots – are the very people who are the most unrepresented in the salons of literature… The sáhityika or the artist has to take the responsibility of enabling them to rise up and sit in the same row with the rest of society, after dusting off the dirt from their bodies…

chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: In special sense, áp means “the process of shaving”. Similarly, va [verbal root] + d́a [suffix] gives us the word va, one meaning of which is also “shaving”.

t: Talking about va, this reminds me of a small story. You must have seen the rows of barbers sitting by the Ganges in Baghbazar [Kolkata city]. Any man who wants a shave squats on his heels in front of one of them and the barber promptly does the act of va [he gives him a shave]. At times, the barber says to his workfellows, “That was the twenty-eighth. Another two and I will call it a day.” In the same manner, you often overhear in the restaurant, “Four teas over there!”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: However, when a well-to-do man approaches the barber, he is offered a brick to sit on. Thus, these roadside barber-shops earned the [amusing] name it́-álián salons because they offer brick [it́ in Bengali] as seats.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: I had noticed that until 1939 or 40, the barbers would use ordinary water to shave their squatting customers and charging them only one paisa. And for those who were offered bricks, they would provide hot, soapy water, and charge two paise.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: In this context, an anecdote about ganja-addicts comes to my mind. When a newcomer joins a group of veteran ganja-addicts, he has to smoke while squatting. The novice is then called a ubu geṋjel [squatting smoker] or an ‘‘apprentice smoker’’. After gaining experience over a probationary period, he has to pass a sort of suitability or efficiency test before he is awarded a brick to sit on. When he earns the right to a brick-seat, he is no longer called a ‘squatting smoker’, but is dubbed an it́-álián-addict.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Once upon a time, some ganja-addicts had gathered for a meeting on the bank of the Bhagirathi River. (I cannot recall if it was the right bank or the left. It would be in Bardwan District if it was the right bank or Nadia District if it was the left).
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: The ganja-addicts met under a coral ( 1 ) tree.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: A number of ‘apprentice smokers’ raised their voices at the meeting demanding to be given the efficiency test. They said that they had not yet been tested for their skill and, thus, were being denied the opportunity to become an it́-álián-addicts. They claimed that their mental development was being throttled and their talent was being suppressed!
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: The leader of the ganja-addicts was Srijukta Bábu Damphát́á Singh. He said, “All right, letʼs hold the test to-day.” He continued: “As you inhale the ganja, you will have to assume a mood. Depending on how dramatic and convincing the mood, you will be awarded a title and a brick.”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: The novices clamoured, “Please explain a bit more, clarify a little what we have to do, so that we can put on a good show and enjoy the drugʼs intoxication event more.”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: The leader said, “Say, for instance, someone assumes the mood of a cow. Then, if somebody puts a hundred rupee currency note in front of him, he will immediately start chewing on it up, or shake his head to and fro, try to gore with his horns and bellow like a cow. Or, say he assumes the role of a pig. ( 2 ) He will then promptly start rooting for edible tubers in the ground nearby, swallow them and grunt ghoṋt ghoṋt ghoṋt. Or, say, someone takes the role of an otter. He will then stand up on his two legs, wringing both his hands together and scurry to dive into the water and catch fish in his teeth. If you ask him his name, he will simply utter bhoṋ… bhoṋ… bhoṋ! We, the veteran ganja-addicts, call this ‘assuming a mood’.”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Then, just as the test was about to begin and the bell about to ring, Lambákarńa, the father of the apprentice-smoker, Ghant́ákarńa Ghoŕoi, suddenly appeared on the scene. In his youth, Lambákarńa had been no stranger to ganja-smoking. On seeing the father, Damphát́á Singh, the leader of the drug addicts, said to Ghant́ákarńa, “Look, there comes your father! If you still remain in the mood of a human being, you will have to answer uncomfortable questions. Youʼd better quickly assume the role of some bird or animal.”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Ghant́ákarńa promptly assumed the mood of a parrot.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Lambákarńa told him, “Why do you roam around all day and smoke ganja? Come home with me. Now it is time for cultivation… the seeds are being sown. Come home with me.”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Ghant́ákarńa puckered up his lips, and chewed on pulses like a parrot and screeched… t́yáṋ… t́yáṋ… t́yáṋ.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Lambákarńa said, “What a clown? Playing the role of a parrot! Iʼll show you what for.”
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Then he caught hold of his sonʼs neck with his teeth, mewing like a tomcat.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

t: Ghant́ákarńa had assumed the role of a parrot, and now the “cat” had pounced on his shoulders! So the “parrot”, true to life, croaked for a while, its shoulder dropping, and and then fell limp. Lambákarńa, the “cat”, dragged Ghant́ákarńa, the “parrot” home.
chapterTitle: The “It́álián” Barbershops

If you find an opportunity, I would suggest you find out from Damphát́á Singh whether, after this incident, Ghant́ákarńa ever came to the addict meets again or not; or if he did come, if he had actually graduated to an expert it́-álián addict. And yes, while you are at it, try to also find out whether the incident took place in Bardhaman or Nadia District!

t: The Sanskrit root shák can also be used in the sense of “mincing something” (as in mincing vegetables) or “cutting something into pieces” (as in chipping betel-nuts). So, the word sha can be used to mean some thing that has been chopped into pieces. For example, chopped betel-nut is called sha-guváka. In ancient times, a nutcracker [yáṋti] was known as sha-yántrika (yántrika > yántia > yáṋti) [yántrika is the adjective form of yantra which means “a device or machine”]. In current Oriya, a yántrika is called guá-yántrika.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Talking of yáṋti or nutcrackers, this reminds of one Shriimatii Put́uráńii Dásii of Baghbazar, the seller of cháṋcii [bitter-tasting] betel-leaves. Do you want to hear about her?
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: It was a small four-legged shop with a tin-roofed top. This was where Shriimatii Put́uráńii Dasii used to chop betel-nuts, prepare and sell betel-leaves. She sold only cháṋcii betel-leaves.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Betel leaf connoisseurs used to regularly flock to her from far and near, from Tollah to Tollygunge, from Belgachia to Bajeshivpur crowding around her shop. She had wonderful dexterity in making betel-leaves with just the right mix of lime and catechu. Although a trifle costly, she put some real betel-nuts in her product – a hundred percent pure betel-nuts and not the adulterated stuff of chopped coconut shells. Her conduct was excellent too. She was never ingratiating but always behaved politely. She used to bring pure betel-leaves every day all the way from Bagnan, garden-fresh so to say, because stale leaves never tasted good. Every client paid her the price she asked for, except Rámt́ahal Singh, the night watchman. Rámt́ahal Singh would casually turn up at her shop at all hours, banging the baton and demand, “Hey, Put́ii, give me a betel-leaf.” Put́uráńii would then sulkily give him one. This man never paid her, as if it were his birthright to get things for free.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Thus Put́uráńii was somehow managing to run her shop and her family. Selling betel-leaves was hardly a profitable proposition. However, in all activities of life, she was exceedingly honest and hardly faced any adverse circumstances.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: One day, she was taken aback to see that Rámt́ahal Singh had not come alone. A few of his country cousins – Rámsurath Singh, Rám Singhásan Singh, Rámbajrang Singh and Rámvecávan Singh – had come with him. Rámt́ahal grabbed fistfuls of prepared betel-leaves for them from Put́uráńiiʼs small metal basin and then took a handful of some chopped betel-nuts from her canister.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: This was too much for Put́uráńii to accept! She cried out, “just because Iʼm a weak and uncomplaining woman, youʼr taking things for granted, arenʼt you?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Then she caught hold of his hand and bit on his wrist with her teeth. She picked up the heavy betel-nutcracker she had bought in Dacca, and beat him on his head several dozen times. Rámt́ahal Singh and his ‘Party Unlimited’ screamed and ran for their lives, crying, ” Oh, my father, Oh my father, what a hell, what a hell is this, oh my father!“ Put́uráńii grumbled to herself, ”They harass me like this just because Iʼm a weak and uncomplaining woman.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The matter did not end there, it went on long after that.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The next morning, as soon as Put́uráńii had opened her shop, Rámt́ahalʼs superior officers and his party arrived. They wanted to know why she had obstructed a policeman in his line of duty by biting on his hand.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Put́uráńii exclaimed, “What do you mean? Line of duty! Obstruction! I cannot make out anything of all this nonsense.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The higher officers said, “Rámt́ahal was carrying out his duty, but you bit him and prevented him from doing just that. Why did you obstruct him? Why?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Put́uráńii said, “Is swooping down on my shop and grabbing fistfuls of betel-leaves by force and stealing betel-nuts part of his job?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The police officers said, “Well, weʼll look into it.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: In due course, the case came up in the court. She had to attend for trial. On the day of hearing, Put́uráńii found the court full of people – it was crowded and noisy. Everyone was curious to see the woman who had bitten a police watchman! The bailiff called out the concerned names one by one.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The court said, “Now call Niilmadhav Ganguly.” The bailiff shouted, “Nirmálii Dáḿgulii present!” three times.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Niilmadhav Ganguly presented himself and his case was heard.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The court then called for Rasiklal Hajra to present himself. The bailiff garbled up the name in his own fashion and shouted, “Rasagolla lál Jháṋjhrá come forward!” three times. Rasiklal Hajraʼs case was then heard.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: After this the court directed Bajrang Paswan to present his case and he duly appeared. The complaint against him was that he had dirtied the roads and did not use the cheap roadside toilets. The judge asked him, “What is your name?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “Bajrang Paswan, Your Honour.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “What do you do?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “I pull a rickshaw, Your Honour.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “Why donʼt you use a cheap toilet? Why do you dirty the roads?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “I have something to say, Your Honour.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “Go ahead.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Bajrang said, “I pull a rickshaw. Cows, buffaloes and horses also pull carts. They donʼt use the cheap toilets, they soil the roads. So do I. Tell me, what wrong did I do, sir?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The judge said, “Heʼs right. Those who pull carts make the roads dirty; they do not use cheap toilets! So where did Bajrang go wrong? As long as there are hand-pulled rickshaws, by what logic can action be taken against a rickshaw puller for soiling the roads? Otherwise, it has to be made mandatory for the cows, buffaloes and horses to use cheap toilets too!” Bajrang Paswan was therefore acquitted, on being found not guilty.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Then it was the turn of Put́uráńii Dásii, the seller of cháṋcii betel-leaves.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The court asked, Are you Put́uráńii Dásii, the seller of pure betel-leaves?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Put́uráńii said, “Why do you waste time by asking me this question? You have called my name because my name was already written on that paper in front you!”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The judge said, “I wanted to confirm that you are indeed that person.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: She looked around and said, “I am the only weak and uncomplaining woman present here. Then why are you looking for Put́uráńii?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: “There is a serious allegation against you,” said the judge, “You obstructed a government employee from doing his duty. Why did you bite his wrist?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Put́uráńii said, “If a thief enters a house to steal and the householder bites his arm, would you call it ”obstructing a government servant in his duty?“ That scoundrel Rámt́ahal used to demand free betel leaves from me every day. He acted as if it were his right! On that day I found he and his party were grabbing a lot of betel-leaves and running away with fistfuls of chopped betel-nuts. I thought, this could never be rightfully his! He was doing this to me because I was a weak, uncomplaining woman; so, I bit on his wrist. Now Mr. Magistrate, you are an honourable man. Tell me what wrong did I do?”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The judge pondered.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: Put́uráńii said again, “And one more point, your Honour.
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The people, who complained to you against me so vociferously, did not tell you the whole truth. Not only did I bite on that thiefʼs wrist, I also hit him on the head with my nutcracker. Please take note of that too.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

t: The judge said, “Considering the case from all angles, it appears that, Put́uráńii is not guilty, so she is acquitted.”
chapterTitle: Was Put́uráńii a Weak Woman?

But the wonder of it is that the same being that considers the waking state the final and supreme truth, also considers the dream state as the final and supreme truth as long as he or she is dreaming. Deep sleep is the state of the experience of nothingness. Thus, despite the impossibility of calling this supreme or final, after waking from this deep sleep one falls into the error of thinking of this recent experience of absence as supreme and final. Actually, the dream state is a combination of subtle experiences collected from the mental world and vibrations collected from the waking state. Those vibrations which are gathered from the crude world oscillate constantly between truth and untruth, but those which come from the mental world are sometimes relative and sometimes non-relative truth. There is little opportunity for vibrational movement in the conviction of absence realized in deep sleep but we cannot reject this as non-existence.
